Referee #1 (Remarks to the Author):

The paper proposes a new approach to understanding and quantifying community stability, essentially taken as the coefficient of variation of combined species responses across a gradient, demonstrating that this approach outperforms simpler descriptors of performance based on single-species or single traits. Overall the paper is nicely put together and written very well. The combination of lit review, simulations, and an experimental test is ambitious and something you rarely see, and the attempt to find a more operational measure of stability is a worthwhile goal. That said, I have a number of concerns and questions:

1. The framing leans heavily on traditional modern coexistence theory, i.e., references to work by May and Allesina in the opening paragraph, which are used to motivate why interactions and interaction networks matter for stability. But those papers are really about species stability in the sense of dynamical stability (composition staying constant), not about biomass output staying constant. What's actually being measured here feels much closer to ecosystem-level stability in a diversity-function sense, and the transition between the two in the intro conflates the two, in a sense setting up this paper under the guise of modern coexistence theory but then transitioning to something else entirely. It also means a big body of work ends up getting skipped, most notably the storage effect and related coexistence theory (e.g. Chesson 1994, 10.1006/tpbi.1994.1013), which is essentially the framework the paper is reinventing in more empirical form. There's a lot of derived mathematical work on the storage effect, how environmental fluctuation maintains true community stability that isn't discussed here at all, and the paper would be much stronger if it demonstrated how its results build on and overcome the existing challenges in this area.

**Framing problem. Defined stability for our study. The storage effect provides an important connection to fluctuating-environment coexistence theory, but asks a different question: how environmental responses and competition allow species to persist. Our question concerns the variability of their aggregate. Response complementarity alone does not establish a storage effect, and we do not claim that CP curves replace this theory.** 

2. Partly because of the above, the literature review is hard to follow and interpret in places. I wasn't sure whether you're restricting to biomass stability (as used in the results here) or species stability (i.e., return to equilibria after perturbation or ability to grow when rare), how you handle traits that act on growth vs traits that parameterise interactions, or how you treat niche vs fitness differences (since combining r and a_ij blurs both). Indeed, around L132 you say species interactions and species responses have rarely been tested together, but both r_i and alpha_ij are central to stability under standard theory and are used throughout stability theory and empirical differences, where interactions give stabilising differences and responses give fitness differences. So I ended up a bit confused about what exactly is being tested and what lit review was actually looking for. More precision in the methods and framing would help a lot, and clarifying exactly what measures of stability are being considered.

**Review limited to the Supplement.**


3. The trait framing in the introduction and in the simulations feels like a bit of a misdirection at times, particularly given the initial framing of stability in the classical species sense. At L80, traits are presented as single things, but classical theory has long been about how multiple traits drive niche and stabilising differences (see Allesina & Levine 2011, 10.1073/pnas.1014428108 for how traits (factors) affect coexistence, or Kraft et al 2015, 10.1073/pnas.1413650112, where multiple traits are explicitly parameterised to separate niche from fitness effects). Framing traits as solely affecting productivity, or rather, simply as summary statistics derived from a performance curve, isn't really accurate to what ecological theory actually does.

4. This carries into the simulations too, which effectively assume a trait only enters through r_i. But traits also affect alpha_ij, and if you take alpha_ij as reflecting niche overlap in some sense, which is typically done, then most of the traditional focus on trials enters through alpha_ij. The simulations and the discussion sidestep this, which feels like an important gap that is left unresolved

5. Related to that, how exactly were the alpha_ii values handled in the simulations? Usually it's the ratio of alpha_ii to alpha_ij that dominates stability, with large diagonals ensuring stability (in the dynamical sense) regardless of ri and alpha_ij, such that alpha_ii is often fixed at 1 for consistency. Was that the case here? A more mechanistic setup would be something like deriving a_ij from trait differences of some kind, which anchors these to a_ii, and would also let you actually probe niche vs stabilising differences. As it stands the sims don't really engage with what stability typically means in the theory, since there's very little integration of niche vs fitness differences, a_ij vs a_ii, or how traits map into either. The focus on traits simply via r_i just doesn’t align with how many community ecologists and functional ecologists think of traits.

6. The results essentially show that your metric correlates with productivity better than SD of optima or mean optima. That's a fine statistical result, but I'm not sure what it buys us. There are plenty of other candidate metrics that would probably also do well (why not MAD or median or MAD/median, why not a multiple regression with SD, skewness, mean, and their interactions?). At this point it becomes a model building exercise for how to describe aggregate performance curves, and while your metric clearly does well, there isn't really a theoretical argument for why it should be the best or optimal or theoretically justified choice. The fact that it works under the simulations and in your experiment is encouraging, but this could partly be an artifact of the LV assumptions and the specific form of interactions used. In regimes with strong stabilising niche differences and weak fitness differences, for example, I'd expect interactions to matter a lot more because performance curves are essentially unimportant (dynamically, at least). It would help if this metric could be linked back to core theory in stability in some way (e.g., via storage effects) to provide a more causal argument for why it should be focused on.

7. I was also surprised not to see more comparisons to traditional stability metrics. I realise some of this traces back to the community vs ecosystem stability issue, but even so, more explicit attention to stabilising vs niche differences in both the sims and the experiment would have gone a long way toward making the case that this approach builds on existing methods.

8. Because the results are CV of biomass, this feels closer to a diversity-function question than traditional ecological stability, and I'm curious how much of what you're seeing is driven by something like selection bias. If one species happens to grow really fast at a particular temperature, community performance at that T is very large, which also skews the CV of performance. I'm not sure this necessarily mathematically will lead to higher stability, but some exploration of these well-known statistical artifacts and how they should feed into aggregate functioning would help put the metric in context.

9. Two quick points: for Fig 4, is the outcome CV of community biomass or just log10? The methods (L469) say CV, so I assume it's just a labelling choice, but worth clarifying. Also, in the equation on L 374, I think the summation should just be over j, not i, so as to align with typical LV where the summation is taken over the competitor with i fixed. Or am I missing something here?

Taking all of this together, I struggle to see where the core novelty sits in its current framing. I again applaud the authors on an ambitious topic of combining a literature review, simulations, and experiments. But if someone's interested in predicting biomass stability and has performance curves in hand, they can already calculate a whole suite of metrics and don't really need to be limited to one. And if they've got morphological or physiological traits beyond aggregate performance optima, they could in principle parameterise an actual LV model and estimate a_ij directly. If they don't have any of that, then the paper needs to engage more deeply with theory to make the case that this metric helps us with our understanding of stability, and/or is a causal driver of ecosystem stability rather than just a useful summary of the community. As it stands it sits somewhere in between, so being clearer about the theoretical framing and intended application of this would help clarify the overall value and novelty of this work.




Referee #2 (Remarks to the Author):

Though the overarching topic is very near and dear to my own research interests, I find the authors' presentation and attempt to demonstrate their arguments very uncompelling. While I understand the motivation to approach the core questions from multiple angles---via a systematic review, model simulations, and analysis of experimental data---I feel that the combination has diluted and weakened rather than strengthened their study overall. Indeed, each of these elements struck me as extremely superficial compared to expectations. I also found a number of the authors' methodological decisions to be extremely challenging to rationalise and/or to have the potential to strongly undermine many of their key claims. I will explain these issues and others in greater detail below in the hope that they are useful for the authors going forward.

As the authors know well, the word "stability" means a myriad different things within the ecology literature. Indeed, there is an argument that, when used without qualifying to which stability someone is actually referring, its use is borderline meaningless. The issue here is that the motivation and exposition of this current manuscript, from the title to conclusion and everywhere in between, hinges critically on the reader knowing precisely how these authors intend to use the term. But by leaving its use largely generic, the onus is left on the reader to determine whether any given mention is consistent with the one that preceded it or whether any given contrast is a comparison of apples with apples or apples with oranges. Consider, for example, the very first sentence of the introduction. The authors cite two different studies that both aim to connect ecological complexity, interaction strengths, and stability; however, their respective definitions of stability are mathematically and statistically completely different. By skipping past or glossing over the underlying differences, these authors run the risk of creating greater confusion rather than greater clarity. Furthermore, ignoring the long-standing differences between different "branches" of stability research in ecology also creates a false dichotomy between "paradigms that prioritise interaction structure and those that emphasise environmental response structure" since researchers who follow either tend to be focused on very different stability "outcomes" in the first place.

Overall, I found the inclusion of the systematic review to be terribly unconvincing. The total number of studies identified is extremely small, and the nature of how those studies are delineated renders the comparisons to be qualitative and thus not necessarily indicative of any statistically meaningful pattern. Without further information, we also cannot use such post hoc analyses to determine why 77 studies "addressed either interactions or species responses". This may purely be a pragmatic decision on the original authors because following one school of thought is a more viable publication strategy; indeed, just because a set of authors chose to follow one paradigm at best implicitly endorses that selected paradigm over all others (i.e., absence of evidence is not evidence of absence). I would recommend removal of this portion of the manuscript altogether. It might perhaps be an interesting contribution on its own, but I see very limited value for it here.

With regard to the simulations and empirical study, there are many facets which concern me regarding the authors' analyses and the extent to which the two perspectives can intuitively build off each other. First and foremost, if the simulations are to be conceptualised as a lens through which to understand these empirical data, why would a discrete-time Lotka-Volterra model be an appropriate description of population dynamics of organisms like ciliates? In my experience, if researchers wished to use the observed dynamics to estimate the parameters of a Lotka-Volterra model (for example, it would be much more common for researchers to fit the time series to a continuous-time model instead (e.g., Carrara et al 2015). This is relevant not only for understanding how fluctuations in T, which create variation in r_i(T), translate mathematically into fluctuations in N, but also whether we expect over-shoot dynamics, damped oscillations, or just smooth relaxation toward equilibrium densities.

Even setting aside the choice of continuous- vs discrete-time models, is it even particularly novel to argue that differential variation in growth rates over temperature will create differential variation in total biomass if temperature fluctuates? I'm not so sure. Presumably after the initial 1000 time steps, the simulated communities have reached equilibrium (but see my later point about equilibrium species richness), at which point N^* = A^-1 r where N* is the vector of equilibrium densities, A is the interaction matrix (and A^-1 the inverse thereof), and r is the vector of growth rates at T = 20. If the temperature then begins to fluctuate, the interaction matrix will then "convert" fluctuations in r into fluctuations in N (and if the fluctuations in T are big and quick enough the system may never return precisely to equilibrium densities). This is all fully consistent with results already shown elsewhere in much greater detail (e.g., Loreau & Mazancourt 2008 and Loreau & Mazancourt 2013). The key addition here seems, to me, to be little more than allowing the strength of species' responses to fluctuating environmental conditions (sigma_ei sensu Loreau & Mazancourt) to be variable.

Moreover, the comparison between community performance curve and community stability, where community stability is the coefficient of variation in total community abundance, appears to me to completely miss the main "point" of the vast majority of studies whose primary emphasis is on the importance of species interactions on emergent ecological phenomena such as local stability, persistence, coexistence, etc. Namely, the "interactions are important" paradigm is less focused on whether the whole community is abundant---in a temporally static world---or variable---in a temporally variable world---but rather which species are more or less abundant in temporally static or temporally variable worlds. Therefore, just like community weighted mean traits are limited in what they can tell us about the different species that make up a specific community (see L73 in this paper or Brown et al 2014; Clark 2016; Peres-Neto et al 2017), CV in total community abundance doesn't tell us very much about the component abundances that make up that total.

In addition, I believe that there is are two potentially pathological deficiencies in the authors' model that confounds much of their analysis for the intermediate and strong interactions. First, the variance of the normal distribution used to parameterise competition coefficients in both scenarios is large enough that it is very probable to sample values < 0 which would be indicative of facilitation and not competition. Second, the mean of the normal distribution in both scenarios is large/strong enough that the species richness after the initial transients is likely much lower than the initial richness from their "experimental design". The methods indicate that this has been "fixed" by introducing a small amount of biomass at each time step (but see one of my minor comments below) which is not really defensible on mathematical nor ecological grounds; competitive exclusion does and can happen in real communities, and artificially preventing it here shouldn't be necessary. Indeed, it wouldn't be necessary at all should the authors have chosen to study the continuous-time version of the model.

Circling back to the broader point building off the historic studies from Loreau & Mazancourt, if fluctuations in r are translated into fluctuations in N as mediated by the inverse interaction matrix A^-1, does it make sense to claim the predictions are "interaction free"? From my perspective, a much stronger evidence base would be to find that species-specific density fluctuations are accurately captured by a model that assumes all interspecific interaction strengths are zero. Or where the authors parameterised a Lotka-Volterra model with monoculture and pairwise experiments (without fluctuating T), observed that some to many pairwise interspecific interaction strengths are inferred to be comparatively strong (e.g., closer to the intraspecific value of 1 than to 0), and yet despite this the "interaction free" model still captured species-specific density fluctuations.

Minor comments

L73) The authors seem to be conflating two different data aggregation processes here into one, and I think for clarity it helps to explain both to the reader. The first is the idea that individual species have continuous environmental response curves, but that we can summarise these through a single value (e.g., T at the optimum). The second is the idea that, given multiple species, all we need to know is the mean of these single values across all species. Both have the potential to be misleading or to throw away useful data.

Fig 1) I think it would be helpful to see example fluctuating time series of T at the top of the middle and rightmost columns. Also, the thick black lines cannot be consistent with the authors' definition of CommunityPerformance(T) since the maximum values should not be capped at 1.

L370) Why is the ranger package being cited regarding Lotka-Volterra models?

L386) The methods indicate that a small unit of biomass is added at each time step. At a minimum, the authors should declare this value explicitly. That said, the code available in the github repository indicates that a small value was actually added to r (https://github.com/opetchey/community.simulator/blob/9770f60d31ac6fca7015013e3edd0240045ba13a/R/simulator_lv.R#L46). In either case, this should not be necessary should the authors follow my suggestion and move to a continuous-time model.

References

Carrara et al 2015 https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12363

Clark (2016) https://doi.org/10.1002/ecy.1453

Loreau & Mazancourt 2013 https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.12073

Referee #3 (Remarks to the Author):

This manuscript by Polazzo et al. describes a novel trait based metric called a “community performance curve” which the authors describe as a powerful tool to describe community stability. I believe the metric the authors describe is novel and extremely useful, solves some problems with many trait based metrics, and has the potential to fill a niche within community ecology. I have, however, some major issues with the framing of the paper that make it difficult for me to assess how this tool fits into the existing literature and whether or not it provides what the authors market it for.
1. The authors frame this metric as one that resolves a long-standing debate in the ecological literature between whether community stability is driven by “interactions” or “species responses” but it is very difficult to tell what the authors mean with these terms. They remain undefined with few examples given even when discussing the theoretical model. I am actually not even sure if I agree with this framing of the paper because many of the more recent studies of community stability appear to me to be relatively interaction neutral, depending on the authors definition of interaction here, and include terms for species responses like species asynchrony and population stability. For example – the partitioning scheme of Shaopeng Wang or the paper from Zhao et al. in 2023 which found that compensatory dynamics were not particularly strong drivers of community stability. In order for me to understand where this effort fits, it would be helpful if clear definitions and examples were given so that I can at least place this effort in a relatively crowded literature. Right now – none of these other efforts are cited, partially understandable given the Nature citation limit, which gives the impression that this is based on a relatively out of date premise. The sentence that really highlights this for me is on lines 62-64 given the above citations and without really understanding what the authors mean by interactions.
2. I am missing some key context as to how only using trait moments would provide a key limitation to understanding species responses. Why are breadth, height, asymmetry, etc so important for predicting species responses to the environment? What information do they provide? There is also a difference between the bottleneck being that information is being based on trait “moments” and information being based on single traits. Both of which are important points but are mixed in the paragraph on lines 72 to 82. I actually find this argument more compelling as a problem to be solved than resolving the “long-standing debate” between is it interactions or species environmental responses. There are many places where this metric can be useful outside of just thinking about stability and eliminating the argument re: interactions vs. species responses would save the authors valuable space to be able to frame and introduce this metric in a way that is more understandable.
3. I don’t fully understand how using a trait-based metric can represent the species response to the environment WITHOUT interactions. The environment in the case of any organism will also include the sum total of all interactions with the other organisms around. Is it about the choice of trait perhaps? I would argue any trait will have some signature of interaction even if we don’t know what that signature looks like.
4. Right now – the authors jump directly into the perceived debate in the stability literature but I found the missing context for this quite jarring. The last paragraphs of the discussion do a really good job of summarizing why studies like this are important and especially for a general readership including this at the beginning will feel less like this paper is about an internecine struggle.
5. If I had to guess based on the search terms – I would guess that the literature review is likely missing quite a bit of the literature that sits within the biodiversity-ecosystem functioning literature. These papers tend to be quite interaction agnostic and may be why I feel a bit uncertain about the premise of the debate in the introduction especially since the paragraph on lines 55 to 60 introduces the biodiversity-stability relationship.

Minor comments:
Line 51 – damped should be dampened

Lines 59-60 – Neither insurance effects nor portfolio effects defined – maybe remove?

Maybe include a theoretical figure that shows what you mean when you say that species responses INDEPENDENT of interactions is likely to influence stability.

Lines 237-240 – This is a really good point and maybe should even be moved up into the intro. All of our measures of interactions are abstractions so we may be estimating them poorly.
